title: Many 18-month-olds handed over an object an unfamiliar adult was reaching for
summary: In a 2007 experiment, 18-month-olds handed an out-of-reach pen to an unfamiliar adult who was reaching for it, and a reward did not raise the rate.
body: Warneken, Hare, Melis, Hanus, and Tomasello tested 36 infants at 18 months. An adult's pen was placed where the infant could reach it and the adult could not. Helping was handing the pen over. Infants helped more when the adult reached than when the adult looked without reaching, and offering a reward did not change that pattern. Sixteen of eighteen infants in the reaching conditions helped at least once. Most of the infants' helping acts came before the adult called the child's name. The task is one out-of-reach object in a lab, not sharing toys at home, and the paper also tested chimpanzees, which is a separate comparison.

sources.title: Spontaneous altruism by chimpanzees and young children
sources.author: Felix Warneken, Brian Hare, Alicia P. Melis, Daniel Hanus, and Michael Tomasello
sources.note: Supports Experiment 1 with 36 infants at 18 months: more handing-over when the adult reached, no reward effect, and 16 of 18 reaching-condition infants helped at least once. CC BY 4.0. Paraphrased.
